criteria.title: Inflated importance
criteria.description: The text claims that ordinary details stand for, or add to, some bigger trend, legacy or debate.
criteria.question: Does the passage claim that small or everyday details show a bigger trend, legacy or debate, in stock phrases?
criteria.source: Content: undue emphasis on significance, legacy, and broader trends
criteria.plain: The writer makes plain things sound important. A date or a name is said to show a bigger trend or a lasting legacy. Nothing in the text backs this up. Example: "This street name highlights the wider story of the town."

criteria.title: Shallow commentary tacked on
criteria.description: A sentence ends with an "-ing" phrase that adds vague comment about meaning or impact, often with no named source.
criteria.question: Do sentences end with an "-ing" phrase giving vague comment on impact or meaning, such as "highlighting its influence"?
criteria.plain: A sentence states a fact. Then an "-ing" phrase adds a vague comment on what it means. The comment has no proof behind it. Example: "The park opened in 1990, reflecting the city's growth."

criteria.title: Advertising tone
criteria.description: The writing reads like a brochure or press release, with stock praise and a constant positive slant.
criteria.question: Does the passage sound like an advert or travel guide, using stock praise instead of a neutral tone?
criteria.plain: The text praises its subject like a brochure. The praise uses the same stock words each time. A neutral writer would just state the facts. Example: "A vibrant town with a rich heritage and stunning views."

criteria.title: Vague links between things
criteria.description: Two things are said to be "connected to" or "associated with" each other, instead of stating the plain relationship.
criteria.question: Does the passage say things are "connected with" or "associated with" each other instead of stating the plain relationship?
criteria.source: Content: vague expression of connection or association
criteria.plain: The text will not say how two things relate. It says they are "connected with" each other. A clear writer would say who did what. Example: "She was associated with leadership at the firm," not "She led the firm."

criteria.title: Vague sources and inflated opinion
criteria.description: An opinion is credited to unnamed experts or "scholars", or a view from one source is shown as widely held.
criteria.question: Does the passage credit opinions to unnamed experts, critics or scholars, or present one view as widely held?
criteria.source: Content: vague attributions and overgeneralization of opinions
criteria.plain: The text says "experts" or "critics" believe something. It never names them. One view may be made to look like many. Example: "Many scholars agree that the play is a masterpiece."

criteria.title: Formula for challenges and future
criteria.description: A paragraph says "despite its strengths, it faces challenges", then ends on a hopeful note about the future.
criteria.question: Does the passage follow the formula "despite its strengths, it faces challenges" and end with a hopeful outlook?
criteria.source: Content: outline-like conclusions about challenges and future prospects
criteria.plain: A section follows a set pattern. It starts with "Despite its good points" and names some problems. It ends with a hopeful look ahead. Example: "Despite this, the club has problems, but new plans may help it grow."

criteria.title: Overused AI words
criteria.description: Many words that chatbots favour appear close together, such as "delve", "tapestry", "pivotal" or "underscore".
criteria.question: Does the passage use many words that chatbots overuse, such as "delve", "tapestry", "pivotal", "underscore", "showcasing" or "vibrant"?
criteria.source: Language and grammar: high density of "AI vocabulary" words
criteria.plain: Some words show up far more in chatbot text. One or two prove nothing. A crowd of them is a strong sign. Examples are "delve", "pivotal", "tapestry" and "vibrant".

criteria.title: "Serves as" instead of "is"
criteria.description: Plain "is", "are" or "has" is swapped for grander verbs such as "serves as", "stands as", "features" or "boasts".
criteria.question: Does the passage use "serves as", "stands as", "features", "boasts" or similar instead of plain "is", "are" or "has"?
criteria.source: Language and grammar: avoidance of basic copulatives
criteria.plain: The text avoids the simple words "is" and "are". It picks grander phrases. Example: "The hall serves as a venue and boasts a large stage," not "The hall is a venue and has a large stage."

criteria.title: "Not just X, but Y" contrasts
criteria.description: The text sets up a contrast that fixes a view nobody held, such as "not only X but Y" or "it's not X, it's Y".
criteria.question: Does the passage often use contrasts like "not just X but Y", "it's not X, it's Y" or "Y rather than X"?
criteria.plain: The writer sets up a contrast that fixes a view nobody held. The pattern is "not just X, but Y" or "it's not X, it's Y". One use is normal. Many uses are a sign. Example: "It's not just a school, it's a community."

criteria.title: Lists of three
criteria.description: The text keeps grouping things in threes, such as three adjectives or three short phrases, to sound complete.
criteria.question: Does the passage keep grouping things in threes, such as three adjectives or three short phrases?
criteria.source: Language and grammar: rule of three
criteria.plain: The writer groups items in threes again and again. It can be three adjectives or three short phrases. It makes thin ideas sound full. Example: "fast, reliable, and easy to use."

criteria.title: Emoji as decoration
criteria.description: Emoji are placed before headings, bullet points or key phrases as decoration.
criteria.question: Does the passage put emoji in front of headings, bullet points or key phrases as decoration?
criteria.plain: Small pictures called emoji are used as decoration. They sit in front of headings or list items. Plain human prose rarely does this. Example: "🚀 Key features".

criteria.title: Curly quotation marks
criteria.description: Curly quotation marks and curly apostrophes are used where straight ones are normal, or the two kinds are mixed.
criteria.question: Does the passage use curly quotation marks or curly apostrophes, or a mix of curly and straight ones?
criteria.source: Style: curly quotation marks and apostrophes
criteria.plain: Some chatbots type curly quotes and apostrophes. Plain typing makes straight ones. A mix of both is a stronger sign. Curly quotes alone prove nothing, because many word tools make them. Example: it’s, not it's.

criteria.title: Notes aimed at the user
criteria.description: The text includes messages meant for the person who asked, such as offers of help, advice or instructions to edit.
criteria.question: Does the passage include messages meant for the person who asked for it, such as offers of help, advice or editing instructions?
criteria.source: Communication intended for the user: collaborative communication
criteria.plain: The text still holds chat with the user. It may offer help or give a tip. It may tell the user to edit or delete something. This is not content for readers. Example: "I hope this helps! Let me know if you want changes."

criteria.title: Disclaimers about missing information
criteria.description: The text says information is not publicly available, or warns that a claim is only symbolic or speculative, rather than stating facts.
criteria.question: Does the passage claim that information is not publicly available, or warn that a source or claim should be treated as speculative rather than firm?
criteria.source: Communication intended for the user: hedging disclaimers about source availability and recommended usage
criteria.plain: The text says the facts are "not publicly documented". Or it warns that a claim is only "symbolic", not "verified". Then it often guesses what the facts might be. Example: "Details are not widely available, but are likely to be modest."

criteria.title: Blank fill-in-the-gaps text
criteria.description: Template placeholders were left in, such as square-bracket labels, "(Add your link here)" or dates like "2025-xx-xx".
criteria.question: Does the passage contain unfilled placeholders, such as bracketed labels like "[Name]", "(Add your link here)" or dates like "2025-xx-xx"?
criteria.source: Communication intended for the user: phrasal templates and placeholder text
criteria.plain: The chatbot left blanks for the user to fill in. The user forgot to fill them. Example: "Dear [Recipient's Name]" or "Website: (Add link here)".
